title: The First Breadth
passages:
The stair ended in a room with a low vault, and there the water was born. It came out of the wall at shoulder height, leaning rather than falling, a hand's width of black water sliding from a crack into a channel cut to carry it; the channel ran back down the steps they had climbed and became the river.

Ilka stepped into the channel. It was ankle-deep and cold enough to hurt. This was the first breadth, the width she had promised to cross and could no longer remember promising. Her legs remembered. They went weak under her and she put a hand on the wall to keep standing.

Above the crack, names were cut into the stone in a column, soft and rounded at the top where the oldest were, sharpening toward the floor. The lowest was fresh. She read it with her fingers before she read it with her eyes. MÁRK VASS.

Behind the stone something clicked, small and exact, a latch turning over. Ninety-five to ninety-six.

"It's stopped pulling," Márk said. He was still on the dry step with Ákos against his shoulder. "It stopped because it has me now."

"No." Ilka put both hands into the water at the mouth of the crack, and the cold went up her arms and made her teeth ache. "It has a word on a wall. It doesn't have you."

She drew breath. Márk understood half a beat too late and lunged for her, but she was already speaking, and the syllable went into the water and did not come back. "Ilka."

Nothing clicked. Then it did. Ninety-seven. Under Márk's name a new line appeared, cut wet and clean and still filling: ILKA.

Márk took her by the shoulder and turned her. His face was white. "What did you give it?"

She stood in the channel and reached for her mother's face the way she had reached for the voice and found nothing. There was a shape with the shape taken out of it, and behind the shape only the room, the water, the boy on the step. "Something with a face," she said. "I don't know yet what."

Márk knelt in the water then, boots flooding, and pressed the cord at his wrist against hers. The cold jumped between them, and for a moment she had her mother's hand on her head, the weight and warmth of it, no face and no voice but the hand, given back and not paid for. He held it there until she stopped shaking. Then he stood, lifted Ákos, and said, "The crack widens higher up. We go while it's still narrow enough to stand in."
